passages.happening:
The Philistines carry the captured ark from Ebenezer to Ashdod. They bring it into the temple of their god Dagon and set it beside his statue (verses 1-2).

“When the people of Ashdod got up early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and returned him to his place” (verse 3).

The next morning it happens again, and worse. Dagon lies fallen on his face before the ark, ‘with his head and his hands broken off and lying on the threshold. Only the torso remained’ (verse 4).

“That is why, to this day, the priests of Dagon and all who enter the temple of Dagon in Ashdod do not step on the threshold” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 4 ended in despair: the ark taken, Eli and his sons dead, the glory gone. Now the story crosses the border into Philistine land, where no Israelite is present at all. There is no army, no priest and no prophet. The LORD defends his own honor.

When one nation defeated another in the ancient world, it often carried off the images of the defeated gods and set them in the victor's temple, as a sign that the conquered god now served the winning one. The Philistines treat the ark this way. They set it beside Dagon, like a captive attending their god.

The scene turns that picture upside down. Dagon falls face down before the ark, in the posture of a worshiper or a defeated servant. His people have to pick him up and set him back in his place. The second morning his head and hands lie broken on the threshold. In the ancient world, cutting off the head and hands of a defeated enemy was a way of showing total victory.

The telling is close to satire. A god who has to be lifted and set in place, and then cannot even stay whole, is no god at all.

Dagon was an old god of the wider region, known in texts from Mari and Ugarit long before the Philistines came. Most scholars now link his name with the word for grain, and the old idea of a fish-god is largely given up. The Philistines seem to have taken him up after they settled in Canaan. Judges places a temple of Dagon at Gaza, and much later, in the second century BC, the book of 1 Maccabees records that Jonathan the Maccabee burned the temple of Dagon at Ashdod.

The custom of not stepping on the threshold, still kept ‘to this day’, shows that the narrator knew a practice at that temple. Thresholds were widely treated as places of spiritual danger in the ancient world.
passages.later:
The prophets mock idols in the same way, gods that must be carried and cannot save: ‘They lift it to their shoulder and carry it along; they set it in its place, and there it stands, not budging from that spot’ (Isaiah 46:7). A psalm says of such gods, ‘they have hands, but cannot feel’ (Psalm 115:7).

Zephaniah condemns ‘all who leap over the threshold’ (Zephaniah 1:9), which many take to mean a custom like the one at Dagon's temple.
passages.asks: Dagon had to be picked up and set back in his place, twice. Ask what in your life you keep propping up, though it cannot stand on its own. And ask what it means that God did not need Israel's help to defend his name.

passages.t: The heavy hand of the LORD
passages.happening:
“Now the hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod and its vicinity, ravaging them and afflicting them with tumors” (verse 6).

The people of Ashdod decide the ark cannot stay, ‘because His hand is heavy upon us and upon our god Dagon’ (verse 7). They call together the rulers of the Philistines, who decide to move it to Gath (verse 8).

At Gath the LORD's hand is against the city too, ‘throwing it into great confusion and afflicting the men of the city, both young and old, with an outbreak of tumors’ (verse 9).

They send it on to Ekron, and the people of Ekron cry out, “They have brought us the ark of the God of Israel in order to kill us and our people!” (verse 10). They call the rulers together again: “Send away the ark of the God of Israel. It must return to its place, so that it will not kill us and our people!” (verse 11).

“Those who did not die were afflicted with tumors, and the outcry of the city went up to heaven” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Ashdod, Gath and Ekron were three of the five chief Philistine cities, with Gaza and Ashkelon. Ashdod lay near the coast. Ekron, usually placed at Tel Miqne, and Gath, usually placed at Tell es-Safi, lay further inland, closer to Israel. All three have been excavated, and they show the Philistines' own way of life in the Iron Age. Each city had its own ruler, and the rulers of the five acted together on matters that touched them all, as they do here.

The key word is hand. The LORD's hand is heavy on the cities, and Dagon's hands lie broken on the threshold. Israel had been given into the hand of the Philistines. Now the Philistines learn whose hand is strong.

Heavy is the same Hebrew root as glory. Ichabod's mother mourned that the glory had departed from Israel. The weight of God's presence has not gone. It is pressing down on the Philistines.

What the tumors were is not certain. The word probably means swellings. Because rats are mentioned in the next chapter, many have suggested an outbreak of bubonic plague, which rats spread and which causes swellings, but the text does not allow certainty.

The ark is passed from city to city like something too hot to hold. The chapter ends with a city's cry going up to heaven, the way Israel's cry went up from Egypt.
passages.later: The plagues of Egypt are the background. There too ‘the hand of the LORD’ struck a nation that held what belonged to God (Exodus 9:3), and there Israel's ‘cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God’ (Exodus 2:23). Here it is the Philistines who cry out.
passages.hard:
Is it fair that ordinary people in the Philistine towns suffered for what their rulers and army did with the ark?

The plague strikes the men of the cities, young and old, not only the soldiers or rulers who took the ark, and modern readers feel the problem. Several things are said in reply. The ancient world understood a community as bound together, and the whole city had received the ark as a trophy and honored Dagon above the LORD. The suffering ends when the ark is sent back, which suggests its purpose was to make the Philistines acknowledge the LORD and not to destroy them. Some readers stress that the Philistines had a clear way out and were not trapped. Others admit that the text simply describes judgment falling broadly, as it often does in history, and that the Bible elsewhere wrestles openly with the suffering of the innocent.

The chapter's main concern is the unmasking of a false god. But the question of a whole people suffering for its leaders is a real one, and Scripture does not always resolve it neatly.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The Philistines passed the problem from city to city instead of asking what it meant. Ask what trouble you keep moving along rather than facing. And ask whom you might blame, too quickly, for a suffering that may not be theirs to carry.
